newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end mixed, spread trading active.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end mixed, spread trading active.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended a quiet session mixed on Tuesday with spread trading noted ahead of first notice day for deliveries, traders said.

"The soybean market really took a breather," said Joel Karlin, analyst with Everen Securities. "There wasn't much news. People are waiting till Thursday (for USDA's weekly export sales)," Karlin said. "If there's a couple more weeks when the crush and export are above 30 (million bushels combined), we'll need to make new highs," he added.
Funds spread roughly 15 million bushels on the day. Floor sources said the moves were to close out May positions.
The market took in stride comments by Willard Sparks, head of Memphis-based analytical firm Sparks Companies. He predicted U.S. new crop soybean production would reach 2.6 billion bushels this year.
Sparks also forecast July futures would climb to $9.00 per bushel, possibly as high as $9.75, while November slid. That would push the July/November spread over $2.00, premium July.
The July/November spread closed at $1.75-1/4, premium July, up 1/2 cent from Monday's close.
Soybeans ended 1-3/4 cents per bushel higher to one cent lower with May down 3/4 at $8.67-1/2.
November had led soybeans up earlier in the session, driven by ideas spring seedings were not proceeding as quickly as expected.

Floor sources pointed to USDA's weekly crop report released Monday which showed corn plantings were 18 percent complete, below expectations for at least 20 percent. USDA has not begun listing national soybean planting progress.

Forecasts called for rains this week in parts of the U.S. Midwest which should put a damper on corn and soybean plantings. Two rain systems were expected to sweep through the U.S. Midwest this week, with the first due late Tuesday.

Old crop contracts drew strength from renewed talk China was looking to buy U.S. and South American soybeans. Some trade sources have said China was willing to pay a premium for U.S. soybeans to avoid South American shipping delays and because of low oil content in Brazilian soybeans.

"Even with the premium the U.S. soybeans have to South American origin, we continue to do business," Karlin said. "We're not rationing enough to make sure we have 125 million bushels of soybeans at the end of the crop year."
On the day, Smith Barney sold 2.0 million bushels each July and November, traders said.
Goldenberg-Hehmeyer, ING and Iowa Grain each bought 1.0 million July, pit sources said.

Spread trade was the featured action on the day. Smith Barney spread eight million bushles August/May at 20-1/2 to 21-1/2 cents, premium May, Cargill Inc spread two million May/July at two to 1-1/2 cents, premium May, and Refco Inc spread two million July/May at two cents.
Soybean volume was estimated by CBOT at 62,000 contracts, compared with Monday's actual volume of 83,134 contracts.
